newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan democracy shaky despite frequent polls.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan democracy shaky despite frequent polls.

text.p: Democracy in Pakistan, ruled by the military for 24 years of its 50-year life, remains fragile despite four elections in the past 12 years, analysts say.
Pakistanis go to the polls again on February 3 amid gloom and national soul-searching that have soured plans to celebrate this year's golden jubilee of half a century of independence.
The austerity-minded caretaker government, installed by President Farooq Leghari after he sacked Benazir Bhutto, has cut back on her lavish ideas, opting for more modest festivities.
Prime Minister Meraj Khalid has been at the forefront of the doomsayers who say that Pakistan has much to be modest about.

"I think we should be ashamed of ourselves instead of celebrating the golden jubilee," Khalid said this month. "Looking back at what we have done in the past 50 years, do we have the right to indulge in...celebrating?"
Much of the angst has focused on the value of an avowedly democratic system that has repeatedly failed to deliver good governance desperately needed by a fractious nation.
"Pakistan's political world is round. This is why 50 years' travel has taken its politics nowhere," wrote columnist Syed Talat Hussain in the English-language daily The News.
"It is still dirty, muddy and confusing," he said, noting the lack of public enthusiasm and the political mud-slinging characterising the current, personality-focused campaign.
This election, like earlier ones, is flawed by the failure of successive governments to hold a national census since 1981.
Given substantial migration from countryside to city in the intervening years, this means cities are badly under-represented in a political system dominated by big feudal landowners.
Another reason for widespread voter apathy may be a sense of futility due to the failure of any elected government to complete its five-year term since martial law ended in 1985.

Each government, apart from periodic caretaker administrations, has been removed by presidents wielding controversial powers to dissolve the National Assembly (lower house), using the Eighth Amendment to the constitution.

Leghari, a one-time Bhutto loyalist who had sworn never to dismiss an elected assembly, did just that on November 5, saying that corruption, nepotism and other abuses had brought Pakistan to the brink of economic ruin and systemic collapse.
He insisted that elections take place 90 days later as laid down in the constitution, but promised that an anti-corruption drive would deter tainted politicians from contesting them.

No top politician has been barred. Media reports say several cases have been shelved to ensure that the two big parties -- Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party and Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League -- had no pretext for boycotting the polls.
The religious Jamaat-i-Islami party is the only significant force to declare a boycott, saying that corrupt politicians must be brought to book before credible elections can take place.
For Paula Newberg, an American academic from Georgetown University with a special interest in Pakistan, the "accountability or elections" debate creates a false dichotomy.

"In fact, you can't have a democratic system without an ongoing sense of accountability," she told Reuters. "There are laws in place in Pakistan that would allow for accountability to take place -- if people were willing to enforce them."
Newberg said that merely holding elections, as Pakistan has shown its ability to do, was no guarantee for democracy.
"To be democratic, you have to act that way, and there is very little to suggest that in the last eight or nine years the Pakistan government has been a democratic government," she said.
Pakistan had its first taste of elections after eight years of martial law when military ruler President Zia-ul-Haq held non-party polls in 1985. Major parties boycotted the exercise.
Muhammad Khan Junejo, though handpicked as prime minister by President Zia, created his own PML faction and showed too much independence for the general's taste. He was sacked in 1988.

Zia died in an unexplained plane crash soon afterward and the PPP took a triumphant revenge at the polls, bringing Benazir Bhutto to office 11 years after Zia toppled and later executed her father and the PPP's founder, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto.
Benazir survived in power for only 20 months against a hostile political and military establishment and was duly removed by then president Ghulam Ishaq Khan.
Sharif came to power after the 1990 election, which Bhutto complained had been rigged. Thirty months later, Sharif fell foul of the president, who fired him on corruption charges.
The Supreme Court overturned the dismissal, but Sharif's reinstated government lasted only a few months before the army chief brokered a deal under which Sharif and the president quit.
The 1993 elections brought Bhutto back to power. Leghari, her nominee, became president -- and her eventual nemesis.
